evidence_quotes.quote: Using social theory, this study examines structural and agential dimensions of power manifested during the establishment process of a water user association in the Northwest Province of South Africa.

A distribution infrastructure of open canals built in the 1950s transports this water to the commercial irrigation farms. This system is operated by the Department of Water and Sanitation local office next to the dam; however, it does not extend to traditional communities in the study area.

Subsequently, water allocations for productive purposes are still tied to land ownership despite the intentions of the NWA 1998 to separate the two and end the system of riparian rights, which advantaged the white minority of commercial irrigation farmers.
Field research was carried out between January and April 2011 with additional site visits in 2015.

The lead author attended the final establishment meeting of the WUA in 2011 (but meetings have taken place prior to this one) in the study area and documented the following narrative. It is important to note at this stage that the establishment of this WUA to date has not been successful.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines integrated water resources management (IWRM) and the attempted establishment of an agricultural Water User Association (WUA) governing surface-water allocations from the Marico-Bosveld Dam and open irrigation canals for productive/agricultural purposes (commercial irrigation, emerging farmers, and subsistence agriculture/livestock), rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (Exclusion Criterion 7). Municipal drinking water is mentioned only once in passing as background context.
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this study WOULD satisfy Criterion 2 because it examines legal, procedural, and institutional governance factors (the National Water Act 1998 including 'existing lawful use' entitlements tied to irrigated land ownership, the National Water Resource Strategy 2, DWAF 2007 WUA establishment procedural guidelines, and institutional power asymmetries). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, Criterion 2 is NOT met because these rules and governance processes do not directly govern household or community water or sanitation service access; instead, the paper examines stakeholder power asymmetries in establishing an IWRM collaborative institution (an agricultural WUA) for bulk irrigation/productive water resources. Because Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 also fail, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical case study combining systematic document analysis of legislation/policy with primary fieldwork (2011 and 2015), including semistructured and focus-group interviews with 48 participants, transect walks, and direct observation of the final WUA establishment meeting.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports procedural exclusion and power asymmetries in stakeholder participation during WUA establishment meetings, non-approval/failure of the WUA establishment process, and lack of access to dam/canal water for agricultural/productive purposes; does not measure or report outcomes of household or community domestic water supply or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies qualitative case study design, study area and sample (48 interview/focus-group participants across national/regional DWS officials, commercial farmers, emerging farmers, local Bahurudshe rural community members, and civil society actors in the Groot Marico subcatchment), governance/power factors, and WUA establishment/productive water allocation outcomes.

study_design: Qualitative case study (document analysis, semistructured and focus-group interviews, transect walks, and direct meeting observation)
population_and_sample: Stakeholders in a proposed agricultural Water User Association in the Groot Marico subcatchment, Crocodile (West)-Marico Water Management Area, Northwest Province, South Africa; 48 semistructured and focus-group interview participants (including 4 commercial farmers, 4 emerging farmers, 18 local community members, DWS national and regional officials, and civil society researchers) plus participants observed at the 2011 WUA establishment meeting
exposure: National Water Act 1998 (including existing lawful use tied to irrigated land), National Water Resource Strategy 2 and DWAF 2007 WUA establishment procedural guidelines, DWS administrative facilitation capacity, and structural/agential power asymmetries between commercial irrigation farmers and emerging farmers/rural communities
outcome: Stakeholder representation and participation in the WUA establishment process, failure/non-approval of WUA establishment, and continued exclusion of emerging farmers and rural communities from productive/irrigation dam water governance
rationale: Excluded (E07 - Wrong service, corresponding to Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Although the paper is an empirical qualitative case study examining South African water law and institutional governance, it investigates IWRM stakeholder participation and power asymmetries in attempting to establish an agricultural Water User Association governing dam/canal water for productive irrigation purposes, not household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access. Municipal drinking water is mentioned only once in passing as background context. Even under the plain broad reading of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.
